name: The Final Cut
epithet: The Twist in the Last Reel

inspiration.film: Psycho / Dressed to Kill / Sleepaway Camp
inspiration.oldScript: The last-reel twist that unmasks the killer as a man in a dress, as if gender variance were the explanation for murder, plus the unwritten kill order that sends the gay friend, the Black friend and the girl who had sex to die first so the 'pure' heroine can live.
inspiration.newLens: Here the twist itself is the villain: a cursed reel that recasts a whole town into those stereotypes. The heroes are the people the script slandered, a trans actress who was promised a real part and a closeted writer facing what his fear wrote, and the Best ending screens the dawn they wrote together, where everyone walks out alive.

logline: At the Glitter Box midnight show, a cursed 1980 slasher reel threads itself, dims the lights and recasts Crystal Street into its ugliest roles. Hit your mark, die on cue, or rewrite the third act.
backstory: In the summer of 1980, schlock producer Barry Kotch shot Lights Out at Crystal Pines at an old scout camp above Glimmer Falls, dressed up as the drowned Camp Crystal Pines, in twenty-six days. Screenwriter Len Carraway, a closeted local English teacher, wrote a story where Nurse Robin leads her campers out of the woods at dawn, and Barry cast Celeste Navarro, a young trans actress from Glory's drag revue, as Robin with a handshake and a promise that this was her big break. Then Barry decided audiences wanted a twist. He cut the dawn ending, shot one close-up of Celeste in a cheap wig and housedress under false pretenses, and spliced it into the last reel as the killer's 'reveal,' with a stranger's voice dubbed over her mouth. He ran the kill order every slasher ran: the gay friend first, then the Black friend, then the girl who went to the boathouse with her boyfriend. Len, terrified of being found out, wrote the monster's monologue in the voice his own shame used on him every night. The film premiered at the Starlight Drive-In that October, and a carload of boys honked at the reveal while Celeste sat three cars away. Barry skipped town owing everyone money, and the answer print ended up in a box of unpaid reels in the Glitter Box projection booth. Six years later the Heartstone has woken it. Now it plays itself at midnight: a projector-beam director with a slate for a face and a megaphone for a voice, recasting the whole street into the script's lies.

centralIssue.title: The twist that was a lie
centralIssue.summary: The Final Cut is the ghost of a story, not a person: a script that slandered real people and taught a town to laugh at them. Celeste was never a twist, Len's shame was never a monster, and the kill order was never a law. Find the call sheet, the original draft and the cut ending, and give the people the script erased the third act they actually wrote.

poster: A towering figure made of pale gold projector light, its face a black-and-white clapperboard slate, a chrome director's megaphone raised, hovering above a glowing 1980s movie palace marquee at midnight, beams of light falling over a crowd of teens and neighbors in Halloween costumes clutching script pages, a strip of film unspooling across the purple sky like a ribbon
portrait: Close portrait of a ghostly figure woven from dusty projector light and drifting film grain, its face a clapperboard slate with chalk scrawl and a cracked hinge, a chrome megaphone held where a mouth would be, scratches and sprocket holes flickering through its body, lit hot magenta from below
endingPhoto: A towering figure of pale gold projector light with a black-and-white clapperboard for a face, raising a chrome megaphone on the stage of an old movie palace at midnight, a beam of light pouring from the projection booth, the velvet curtain parting, teens in the front row throwing popcorn and pointing at the screen
taunts: Places, everyone! You know the order. The order never changes.
Quiet on the set. Rolling. And... ACTION.
Nobody pays to see the ending where everybody lives.
Hit your mark, sweetheart. The audience is waiting for the twist.
That line is not in the script. CUT!

clues.title: The 1980 call sheet
clues.hint: Rewind Video's night-drop slot keeps returning a tape that nobody rented.

encounter.title: Returned by Nobody
encounter.text: Rewind Video's night-drop slot clunks at noon, which it should never do while the store is open. Out slides a VHS of Lights Out at Crystal Pines, the 1980 slasher nobody rents, its box cover a shadow holding a kitchen knife. Zelda Fishbein picks it up with two fingers. "Third time this week. It keeps coming back on its own." Something stiff is folded inside the clamshell.
encounter.art: A battered clamshell videotape case sliding out of a video store's brass night-drop slot at noon, its painted front showing a dark shadow holding a kitchen knife, a 63-year-old woman with a silver-streaked black bouffant and cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain picking it up with two fingers behind the counter, a wall of horror tapes under pink neon, a teenager leaning on the counter, bright daylight through the front window, medium shot

choices.label: Ask Zelda what she knows about this one

success.text: "I know how every monster movie ends," Zelda says. "That one ended wrong." She pries out a folded call sheet: DAY 23, SC. 88, DAWN, ALL CAMPERS EXIT THE WOODS. Top of the cast list: Celeste Navarro, Nurse Robin (LEAD). In the movie on the tape, Nurse Robin never leads anyone out of the woods.
success.art: A silver-haired woman at a video store counter unfolding a yellowed 1980 film call sheet under a desk lamp, a teenager leaning in beside her, horror tapes stacked all around

failure.text: Zelda is ringing up a customer. When you crack the case yourself, the tape leader slithers out and loops around your wrist, and from every TV on the wall a tinny megaphone voice says, "Wrong set, kid. Back to one."
failure.art: A shiny brown ribbon of videotape coiling around a teenager's wrist in a video store, a wall of TV screens all showing the same chalk clapperboard

choices.label: Play the tape on the store monitor and freeze the end credits

success.text: You jog-shuttle to the credits and pause. One line has been scratched off the film by hand, but the ghost of it still glows: Nurse Robin, Celeste Navarro. When you eject the tape, the folded call sheet drops out of the box, as if it had been waiting for someone to look.
success.art: A paused end-credits film still on a chunky 1980s TV monitor, one scratched line of credits glowing faintly, a teenager's hand on a VCR remote, a folded paper dropping from a tape box

failure.text: Every monitor in the store switches to the same shot: a clapperboard snapping shut. "Scene one, take one." Then every screen shows the back of your own head, filmed from a few steps behind you. You do not turn around fast enough to see who is holding the camera.
failure.art: A video store wall of TV screens all showing the back of a teenager's head, the teenager standing frozen in front of them, a clapperboard flickering on one screen

choices.label: Slip the box into your jacket and read it in the back room

success.text: Behind the bead curtain you unfold a call sheet with a coffee ring on it. Scene 88 is circled twice in pencil, and beside it someone wrote: EVERYBODY LIVES. DON'T LET BARRY CUT IT. Under the cast list, a lipstick heart next to the name Celeste Navarro.
success.art: A teenager in a cluttered video store back room reading a coffee-stained 1980 call sheet by the light of a single bulb, a lipstick heart beside one name, a bead curtain behind them

failure.text: Zelda's security mirror catches you, and so does Zelda. She makes you rewind forty tapes by hand as penance. The Crystal Pines box sits on top of the stack the whole time, and you could swear it is laughing.
failure.art: A teenager rewinding a tall stack of VHS tapes by hand at a video store counter, a convex security mirror above, one horror tape box perched on top of the pile

clues.title: Draft three, the real ending
clues.hint: The drama teacher at Glimmer Falls High wrote a movie once, and he never talks about it.

encounter.title: Mr. Carraway Keeps the Lights On
encounter.place: The drama room, Glimmer Falls High
encounter.text: Mr. Len Carraway teaches sophomore English and directs every school play with the house lights on full, because he hates a dark room. He is grading essays under every light in the drama room when you walk in. On his desk is a locked drawer with a strip of masking tape across it, and on the tape, in faded marker: CRYSTAL PINES.
encounter.art: A gentle middle-aged man in a tweed blazer and loosened tie grading essays at a wooden desk in a high school drama room with every light switched on, stage flats and racks of old costumes behind him, a desk drawer sealed with a strip of yellowed masking tape, a teenager standing at the desk holding out a folded sheet of paper, bright even light, medium shot

choices.label: Tell him what his movie is doing at the Glitter Box

success.text: He goes pale and opens the drawer. Draft three, yellowed, the last ten pages in two hands: his typing and Celeste's pencil. "Barry wanted a twist. I gave him one so nobody would look at me too closely. I wrote that monster in the voice I heard in my own head every night. It was never her. It was never anyone. It was a lie I was taught."
success.art: A teacher handing a yellowed movie script to a teenager across a desk, the final pages covered in pencil notes in a second handwriting, his eyes wet, bright classroom light

failure.text: "I don't discuss that picture," he says, too fast. One by one the drama room lights click off until a single spotlight sits on you. On the chalkboard behind him, chalk begins to write by itself: KILL ORDER, and a list.
failure.art: A dark high-school drama room with one spotlight on a teenager, a chalkboard behind them where a floating stick of chalk scrawls a list, a teacher frozen at his desk

choices.label: Show him the call sheet and ask him to read Scene 88

success.text: He reads it aloud. Nurse Robin leads Duane, Kip and Cheryl out of the woods at dawn, all four of them carrying the canoe. His voice breaks on the last line: "Robin looks back once, and laughs, because she made it." He hands you the draft. "Celeste wrote that line. Give it back to her."
success.art: A teacher reading aloud from a worn movie script in an empty high-school auditorium, a teenager listening in the front row, morning light slanting across the stage

failure.text: He starts to read, but the words leave his mouth in a crackling megaphone voice: "Scene 88 is CUT." He drops the pages as if they burned him and asks you, very politely and very shakily, to go to your next class.
failure.art: A startled teacher dropping a script in a drama room, pages scattering, a faint ghostly megaphone shape glowing in the air in front of his mouth

choices.label: Dig through the drama storage room for old scripts

success.text: In a box labeled STRIKE 1980 you find draft three, and paper-clipped to its cover, a note in red grease pencil: Nobody pays for a happy ending. Make the nurse the twist. Make it a guy in a dress, kids love that. B.K. Under it, in Len's typing: This is wrong and I know it. I'm sorry, C.
success.art: A teenager in a cramped drama storage room holding up a yellowed script with a red-penciled note clipped to the cover, cardboard boxes and costume racks under a bare bulb

failure.text: The costume racks roll aside on their own, and a follow-spot swings onto you from somewhere above. "You're not on the call sheet," booms a voice. The door slams, and you spend an hour climbing out through the fly loft with dust in your teeth.
failure.art: A teenager climbing a rope ladder through a dusty theater fly loft, costume racks scattered below, a single spotlight beam pinning them from the dark

clues.title: The can marked DO NOT DESTROY
clues.hint: The woman in the Glitter Box box office knows every regular by name, and she has stopped staying for the midnight show.

encounter.title: Row F
encounter.place: The box office, The Glitter Box Playhouse
encounter.text: Celeste Navarro has worked the Glitter Box box office for five years. She does the crossword in pen, wears cat-eye glasses on a beaded chain, and knows every regular's candy order by heart. This week she leaves before the midnight show and will not say why. When you say the words Crystal Pines, she sets down her pen.
encounter.art: A poised woman in her thirties with dark curls and cat-eye glasses on a beaded chain sitting inside a small glowing glass box office booth at dusk with a newspaper crossword and a pen, the theater marquee blazing with bulbs above her, a teenager at the ticket window, pink and gold marquee light against a purple sky, medium shot

choices.label: Ask her, gently, about Nurse Robin

success.text: She laughs, a real one. "Robin was mine. Barry promised. Then he shot me in a cheap wig 'for a gag reel' and cut it into his ending under some stranger's voice." She leads you to the coat closet: a film can, TRIMS REEL 6 DO NOT DESTROY. "I stole the real ending out of his trash. I could never watch it alone."
success.art: A woman in cat-eye glasses lifting a dented round film can from a theater coat closet and placing it in a teenager's hands, red velvet coats hanging behind them, warm lobby light

failure.text: Her smile goes polite and professional. "Ticket's two dollars, hon." Above you the marquee letters spin on their own and rearrange into THE TWIST, and she pulls the booth shade down without another word.
failure.art: A theater marquee at dusk with its letters spinning and rearranging by themselves, a box office booth below with its shade pulled down, a teenager looking up

choices.label: Buy a ticket and tell her you think the movie lied

success.text: She looks at you for a long time. "Six years I've waited for one person to say that before I did." She closes the booth, takes you up to the projection booth, and shows you the film can she has hidden behind the rewind bench since 1981: the dawn ending, every frame of it.
success.art: A woman and a teenager in a cramped theater projection booth, the woman pulling a dented film can from behind a rewind bench, a hulking projector glowing beside them

failure.text: The ticket machine chatters before she can answer and spits out a stub of its own: ADMIT ONE. EXTRA. DIES IN REEL TWO. Celeste tears it in half, hands you a regular ticket, and stares at the torn halves for a very long time.
failure.art: A paper movie ticket curling out of a brass box office ticket machine, a woman in cat-eye glasses tearing it in half, a teenager watching through the glass

choices.label: Help her through the Saturday rush first

success.text: You work the candy counter in a paper hat, sell four hundred boxes of Choco-Nuggets and settle a feud over the last pickle. At closing Celeste hands you a dented film can like a tip. "You earned the real ending. It's in here. Be careful with her, she's all I kept."
success.art: A teenager in a paper hat behind a busy theater candy counter, popcorn flying, a smiling woman in cat-eye glasses holding out a dented round film can at closing time

failure.text: The popcorn machine erupts like a volcano. Somewhere a megaphone voice shouts, "CUT! Again, from the top!" and the machine does it again. Celeste sends you home buttered and apologetic.
failure.art: A theater popcorn machine erupting in a geyser of popcorn over a panicked teenager in a paper hat, a lobby carpet buried in kernels

signature.title: Places, Everyone
signature.text: The midnight double feature is a rowdy sing-along until the second reel. Then the house lights dim on their own, a clapperboard snaps somewhere in the dark like a gunshot, and two hundred people in the audience turn to look at you. "Line!" booms a megaphone from the projection beam. The person next to you hands you a page of sides. Your name is typed at the top. Your role: EXTRA #4 (DIES).
signature.art: A packed old movie palace at midnight, two hundred audience members turned around in their red velvet seats all staring at one teenager in the middle row who is holding a single typed page, a hard projector beam slicing overhead with the shape of a clapperboard floating inside it, popcorn spilled in the aisle, silver beam light and dark house, wide shot

choices.label: Crumple the sides and improvise

success.text: "Actually," you announce, "EXTRA #4 has a car, and is leaving." The audience howls, laughing at the movie instead of with it. The beam stutters like a scratched record, the house lights pop back on, and Frankie calls intermission over the PA.
success.art: A teenager standing on a theater seat grinning and tossing a crumpled script page, the audience laughing, the house lights blazing back on, a flickering projector beam overhead

failure.text: Your mouth says the line anyway, in someone else's voice: "I'll just go check the boathouse." Your feet start walking toward the exit sign. You get all the way to the alley before the spell snaps and you find yourself somewhere much worse.
failure.art: A teenager walking stiffly toward a glowing red exit sign in a dark theater aisle, a spotlight following them, a script page fluttering from their hand

choices.label: Climb to the booth and pull the projector's plug

success.text: You take the booth stairs three at a time. The projector is running with the booth empty, a reel you have never seen on the feed arm. You yank the plug. The film keeps turning for one long beat after the power dies, then gives up. On the floor: a scatter of quarters and a chalk-dusted slate pencil.
success.art: A teenager yanking a thick power cord from a hulking theater projector in a dim booth, a film reel still spinning, quarters and chalk dust on the floor

failure.text: The booth door is locked from the inside. Through the little porthole you watch the projector thread a fresh reel by itself, and a clapperboard on a stand slowly swivels to face you. It claps once. You feel it in your teeth.
failure.art: A teenager peering through a round porthole window into a projection booth where a projector threads itself and a clapperboard on a stand turns toward the glass

signature.title: The Kill Order
signature.place: Crystal Street, lit like a soundstage
signature.text: Crystal Street has become a set. Klieg lights on the roundabout, cables snaking across lawns, the Heartstone glowing like a key light. The Slate floats over the cul-de-sac in its beam of light, megaphone raised, reading from a clipboard. "First the gay friend. Then the Black friend. Then the girl who went to the boathouse. That's the order. That's always the order." Spotlights swing across the porches, hunting for the neighbors it means.
signature.art: A 1980s suburban cul-de-sac turned into a film set at night, klieg lights on stands, black cables snaking across the lawns, a glowing purple crystal rock at the center under a white key light, a towering ghostly figure woven from pale gold projector light and film grain with a black-and-white clapperboard for a face floating above the street in its own beam, holding a chrome megaphone and a clipboard, spotlights sweeping across the porches, a teenager in the street, wide shot

choices.label: Pull everyone into one spotlight together

success.text: You grab hands and drag neighbors off their porches until you are all crammed into one circle of light, arms linked, too many to cast. The Slate's chalk squeaks and stalls. A slasher only works on people who split up, and this crowd is not splitting up for anybody.
success.art: A crowd of teens and neighbors of every age crammed together arm in arm inside one bright spotlight on a suburban street, a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure above them hesitating, chalk dust drifting

failure.text: The spotlights snap apart like a dealt deck of cards, and every one of them carries someone away into the dark. By the time the lights die, the street is empty except for you and a clapperboard lying in the gutter, chalked: TAKE TWO TOMORROW.
failure.art: Spotlight beams scattering in every direction across a dark suburban street, a lone teenager in the center, a clapperboard lying in the gutter beside them

choices.label: Snatch the clipboard and rewrite the scene

success.text: You leap, grab the clipboard and cross out the whole list. Underneath you write: AND THEN THEY ALL WENT OUT FOR PANCAKES. The klieg lights flicker, confused. Up and down the street, porch lights come on warm and yellow, and somewhere a neighbor actually starts making pancakes.
success.art: A teenager scribbling over a film clipboard under klieg lights on a suburban street, warm yellow porch lights blinking on behind them, a ghostly figure recoiling in its projector beam

failure.text: The pencil writes what it wants, in red, in a handwriting you have never seen. The list gets longer. Your name is on it now, near the bottom, under the words: EVERYBODY ELSE.
failure.art: A pencil writing by itself in red across a film clipboard held by a frightened teenager, klieg lights glaring, a long list running down the page

choices.label: Read the kill order back to it, out loud, like a punchline

success.text: You grab a walkie and broadcast it in your best late-night DJ voice: "Coming up next, the oldest, tiredest rule in Hollywood!" The whole street groans and then cracks up. A rule people laugh at stops being a rule. The Slate lowers its megaphone, sulking.
success.art: A teenager on a suburban lawn speaking into a walkie-talkie like a radio DJ, neighbors on porches laughing, a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure lowering its megaphone in a dimming beam

failure.text: The laughter comes, but it is a canned laugh track, booming out of the klieg lights on cue. The neighbors' faces stay blank. They laugh at exactly the right moments and look at nothing at all.
failure.art: Blank-faced neighbors standing on porches with mouths open in identical laughs, klieg lights glaring, a teenager on the lawn looking around in horror

signature.title: I'll Be Right Back
signature.place: The Starlight Drive-In, closed for the season, midnight
signature.text: The Starlight Drive-In has been shuttered since Labor Day, but tonight its giant screen flickers on while your crew sits in a borrowed station wagon, and the feature is Lights Out at Crystal Pines. The teenagers on screen are wearing your clothes. One of them, in your friend's exact jacket, stretches and says, "I'll be right back." In the back seat, your friend stretches the same way, lips moving in sync, and reaches for the door handle.
signature.art: A deserted 1980s drive-in theater at midnight, rows of metal speaker poles, a wood-paneled station wagon full of teens parked facing a giant flickering screen that shows teens in the exact same jackets, one teen in the back seat stretching and reaching for the door handle while a friend grabs their sleeve, flickering screen light on the windshield, wide shot from behind the wagon

choices.label: Heckle the screen like it's opening night

success.text: "Nobody says that line and lives!" you yell, and the whole wagon joins in, honking the horn and pelting the windshield with popcorn. On screen, the actor freezes mid-step and glares out at the lot, offended. Your friend lets go of the door handle, laughing too hard to go anywhere.
success.art: Teens in a station wagon at a deserted drive-in at midnight honking and hurling popcorn at a giant flickering screen, an actor on the screen frozen and scowling out at the lot, laughter fogging the windshield

failure.text: Your heckle comes out as the next line of the script: "Hurry back." Your friend climbs out and walks to the snack bar, and twenty minutes later you find them behind the counter in a paper usher's hat, sweeping the same square of floor over and over. It takes the whole crew to walk them back to the car.
failure.art: A dazed teen in a paper usher's hat sweeping one square of floor behind a dim drive-in snack bar counter at midnight, a popcorn machine glowing, friends peering in through the doorway

choices.label: Nobody splits up: the whole crew goes with them

success.text: You grab your friend's sleeve and the whole crew piles out together, arm in arm, all the way to the snack bar. Inside, a popcorn machine is popping chalk dust and a clapperboard hangs from a nail. With everyone in one shot, the scene has nowhere to cut. You pocket the quarters from the abandoned register on your way out.
success.art: A crew of teens marching arm in arm into an abandoned drive-in snack bar at midnight, a popcorn machine spilling chalk dust, a clapperboard hanging on a nail, coins glittering on the counter

failure.text: Halfway across the lot the speaker poles scream with feedback and the crew scatters like startled pigeons. For an hour you hear each other's voices calling from the snack bar, the projection hut and the restrooms, every one of them saying, "It's fine, come in here."
failure.art: Teens scattering across a dark drive-in lot between rows of speaker poles, a giant flickering screen looming, the doorways of a snack bar and a projection hut glowing invitingly

choices.label: Get the wagon started and drive out before the reel ends

success.text: The key does the movie thing: click, click, nothing. You were expecting that. You pop the hood, wiggle the battery cable the way every mechanic in Glimmer Falls swears by, and the engine roars. You bounce over the exit ramp as the screen behind you snaps to white with a sound like tearing film.
success.art: A teenager slamming the hood of a wood-paneled station wagon as its headlights blaze on at a deserted drive-in, the giant screen behind snapping to blinding white, gravel spraying from the tires

failure.text: Click, click, click. On the giant screen, the same station wagon sits in the same lot, and a clapperboard drifts down to tap on its driver's window. You look at your own window. Tap, tap. You bail out the far door and run for the road.
failure.art: A frightened teenager behind the wheel of a stalled station wagon at a midnight drive-in, a floating clapperboard tapping on the driver's window, the giant screen above showing the very same car

signature.title: The Cat Scare
signature.place: Your basement, one a.m., lit like a soundstage
signature.text: You go down to the basement for a flashlight and find it has been dressed for a scene: a fog machine hissing behind the furnace, a boom mic dangling from the rafters, and a tape X on the floor in front of the laundry-room door. From nowhere, violins start to build, high and thin and climbing. Every movie you have ever seen says something is about to jump out of that door. Behind you, very quietly, a slate pencil squeaks.
signature.art: A suburban basement at one in the morning dressed as a film set, stage fog curling from behind an old furnace, a boom microphone dangling on a pole from the rafters, a taped X on the concrete floor in front of a closed laundry-room door, a teenager standing on the mark holding their breath with a flashlight, a single bare bulb and a cold spotlight from nowhere, medium shot

choices.label: Hit your mark and yank the door open on the big note

success.text: You yank it open on the shriek of the strings and the neighbors' fat orange cat, Mr. Biscuits, explodes out of the laundry basket, yowling. That was the fake scare. You were ready for the real one, so you spin around and catch the Slate right in its lens with your flashlight. It recoils, blinded, and the violins limp to a stop.
success.art: A fat orange cat leaping out of a laundry basket in a foggy basement, a teenager spinning around with a flashlight beam striking a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure that recoils, a boom microphone dangling overhead

failure.text: The cat explodes out of the laundry basket and you scream so loud the boom mic swings. While you are clutching your heart, the real scare taps you on the shoulder: the Slate, close enough to touch, chalking TAKE ONE across its face. You take the stairs three at a time.
failure.art: A screaming teenager clutching their chest in a foggy basement as an orange cat streaks past, a clapperboard-faced ghostly figure looming right behind their shoulder in a hard projector beam

choices.label: Refuse the cue: sit on the dryer and hum louder than the violins

success.text: You hop on the dryer and hum the theme from a Saturday-morning cartoon, loud and gloriously off-key. The violins try to climb over you, falter, and get stuck going around and around like a broken music box. A jump scare needs a held breath, and you are not holding one. The fog machine sputters out in a sulk.
success.art: A grinning teenager perched cross-legged on a clothes dryer humming loudly in a foggy basement, a boom microphone drooping from the rafters, a fog machine sputtering, ghostly violin shapes tangled in the air

failure.text: The violins swallow your humming and keep climbing until the light bulbs buzz along with them. Then they stop dead. In the silence, the laundry-room door creaks open one inch on its own, and the dark inside waits for you to look. You do not sleep until dawn.
failure.art: A frozen teenager on a basement dryer staring at a laundry-room door creaked open an inch onto deep darkness, bare light bulbs glowing, wisps of stage fog curling along the floor

choices.label: Grab the boom pole and swing it at whatever is behind you

success.text: You yank the boom pole off its hook and swing without looking. It clangs off something hollow, and the Slate's chalk scatters across the concrete like spilled rice. The violins hit a sour note and quit. When the fog clears, your basement is only a basement again.
success.art: A teenager swinging a long boom microphone pole through stage fog in a basement, a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure bursting into a cloud of chalk dust, a stack of laundry baskets toppling

failure.text: You swing, miss, and hook the furnace pipe with an enormous clang that wakes the whole house. By the time your family stumbles downstairs, the fog, the tape and the mic are gone, and you are standing alone in the basement holding a broom, trying to explain.
failure.art: A sheepish teenager holding a broom in a plain basement beside a dented furnace pipe, a family in bathrobes peering down the stairs with flashlights, an orange cat watching from a laundry basket

signature.title: Point of View
signature.place: Crystal Street sidewalks, 2 a.m., through a viewfinder
signature.text: You blink and you are looking through a camera viewfinder, gliding low along the sidewalk at walking speed, while somebody breathes heavily in your ears. The breathing is on the soundtrack. You are the killer's point-of-view shot. The dolly is carrying you toward a lit garage where Manny Alvarado, ten-year-old Ricky's big brother, who runs the follow spot at the Glitter Box, is rehearsing a lip-sync alone in a feather boa. A chalk slate floats at the edge of your vision: FRIEND #1. FIRST.
signature.art: A low view gliding along a dark suburban sidewalk at two in the morning from on top of a film camera dolly running on metal track rails, the edge of a camera viewfinder framing the view, a lit garage ahead where a young man in a pink feather boa lip-syncs into a hairbrush, a floating blank chalk slate glowing beside the track, cold blue night and warm garage light, low tracking shot

choices.label: Wrench the camera around and point it at yourself

success.text: You fight the dolly and swing the lens around until it is staring at you. A killer's-eye shot only works while nobody sees who is holding the camera. Caught on film, the breathing stops with an embarrassed cough, the track buckles, and you tumble onto the Alvarados' lawn as yourself.
success.art: A teenager wrestling a heavy film camera on a dolly to point its lens back at their own face on a dark suburban sidewalk, a lit garage glowing behind them, buckled metal track rails

failure.text: The camera will not turn. It glides you right up to the garage window, and Manny looks up and screams, because from his side of the glass all he can see is you, pressed to the window, breathing hard. You spend the rest of the night apologizing through his mail slot.
failure.art: A teenager pressed against a garage window at night, breath fogging the glass, while inside a startled young man in a feather boa shrieks and drops a hairbrush microphone

choices.label: Break out of the shot, knock, and join his lip-sync

success.text: You stumble off the dolly, knock, and grab the second hairbrush. Manny cues up the tape and the two of you lip-sync the duet of your lives in his parents' garage. Two people in one spotlight make a scene, not a victim, and the floating slate's chalk smears into a heart. Manny makes you promise to come to Saturday's revue.
success.art: Two teens lip-syncing a joyful duet into hairbrush microphones in a cluttered suburban garage at night, one in a feather boa, a boombox blaring, a string of holiday lights glowing, a chalk heart drifting in the air

failure.text: Manny cannot hear you knock over the music. You keep knocking, and the breathing on the soundtrack keeps getting louder until it is your own breathing, and the dolly reverses you all the way to the end of the street. The last thing you see is the slate: TAKE TWO.
failure.art: A teenager knocking on a closed garage door glowing with music and colored light, a dolly track stretching behind them down a dark suburban street, a floating chalk slate hovering at their shoulder

choices.label: Stomp the dolly's brake and derail the shot

success.text: You find the brake with your foot and stomp. The track jumps, the shot shakes like a home movie, and the whole contraption rolls into the Fergusons' hedge with a crunch. The heavy breathing turns to wheezing, then coughing, then silence, and you climb out of the leaves holding a perfectly good flashlight that fell off the rig.
success.art: A film dolly tipped over into a suburban hedge at night with its camera askew, a teenager climbing out of the leaves holding a flashlight, metal track rails scattered across the sidewalk

failure.text: The brake is a gas pedal. The dolly shoots forward, the shot goes woozy and slow-motion, and you find yourself on a completely different street with no idea how you got there, still breathing heavily, which is somehow the most embarrassing part.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager riding a runaway film dolly at speed down an unfamiliar dark street, streetlights smearing into long glowing streaks, a camera bucking on its mount

signature.title: The Twist
signature.place: The Glitter Box stage, after midnight
signature.text: The Slate has rolled a wardrobe rack onto the Glitter Box stage. On it hangs the script's 'Killer' costume: a rental wig, a thrift-store housedress and a rubber knife, the outfit a 1980 producer thought was a punchline. A dress is just a dress. What is frightening is the beam: wherever it lands, it tries to staple that costume to someone and make the audience gasp. "And now," the megaphone purrs, "the twist." The spotlight swings toward you.
signature.art: A theater stage after midnight, a rolling wardrobe rack holding a limp thrift-store housedress, a curly rental wig and a rubber prop knife, a hard white projector beam with a figure of pale gold light and a clapperboard face inside it swinging a spotlight across the stage toward a teenager, a tall drag queen in a sequined robe striding in from the wings, dusty light shafts, wide shot

choices.label: Let Glory take the dress and wear it like a showstopper

success.text: Glory sweeps into the beam, lifts the housedress off the hanger, belts it with a sequined sash, swaps the rubber knife for a microphone and sings "I Am What I Am" to the rafters. The audience gasps, then stands and cheers. A dress was always just a dress. The beam has nothing left to twist, and it flickers out.
success.alone: You sweep into the beam yourself, lift the housedress off the hanger, belt it with a sequined sash, swap the rubber knife for a microphone and sing "I Am What I Am" to the rafters. The audience gasps, then stands and cheers. A dress was always just a dress. The beam has nothing left to twist, and it flickers out.
success.art: A radiant drag queen center stage in a housedress belted with a sequined sash, singing into a microphone in a warm spotlight, a theater audience on its feet cheering, a projector beam fading above

failure.text: The curtain slams down between Glory and the beam before she reaches the rack. The projector rewinds the whole scene with a shriek and starts it again from the top. Glory is furious on your behalf, and you are back where you started, in the spotlight.
failure.alone: The curtain slams down between you and the rack before you can reach the dress. The projector rewinds the whole scene with a shriek and starts it again from the top. Somebody in the balcony boos on your behalf, and you are back where you started, in the spotlight.
failure.art: A heavy red theater curtain slamming down across a stage, a drag queen on one side with hands on her hips, a teenager caught in a spotlight on the other

choices.label: Step into the spotlight and say your own line

success.text: You stand in the beam and say exactly who you are, in your own words, which are in nobody's script. The costume slides off its hanger and lies on the stage like laundry. The Slate's chalk snaps in half with a crack that echoes to the balcony.
success.art: A teenager standing tall center stage in a blazing spotlight speaking out to an empty theater, a housedress fallen in a heap beside a wardrobe rack, a broken stick of chalk spinning in the air

failure.text: The beam pins you like a moth. Line after line pours into your head from the megaphone, every one of them a lie, and it takes everything you have just to keep your mouth shut. You stumble offstage into the wings and keep stumbling.
failure.art: A teenager pinned in a harsh white spotlight with hands over their ears, ghostly script pages swirling around them, a clapperboard-faced figure looming in the beam above

choices.label: Cut the fly rope and drop the painted forest on the Slate

success.text: You haul on the rope lock and the painted Crystal Pines backdrop crashes down through the beam. The Slate shrieks like tearing film and scatters into dust motes. The wardrobe rack tips over, and Frankie, from the wings, drags it off to the costume shop where it belongs.
success.art: A huge painted forest backdrop crashing down through a projector beam on a theater stage, a ghostly clapperboard figure scattering into glittering dust, a teenager gripping a fly rope

failure.text: Wrong rope. A sandbag drops two feet from you and a cloud of sixty years of stage dust swallows you whole. When it clears, the Slate is gone, and so is your jacket, pinned to the rack like a new costume.
failure.art: A teenager coughing in a billowing cloud of stage dust beside a fallen sandbag, a wardrobe rack in the haze with a teen's jacket hanging on it

signature.title: You're All Doomed
signature.place: The Gas-N-Go on Quarry Road, 11 p.m.
signature.text: You pull into the Gas-N-Go for a Bolt Cola, and old Mr. Hensley from the bowling alley lurches out from behind the ice machine in a trucker cap and grabs your sleeve. "You're all doomed!" he croaks. "Crystal Pines has a death curse!" Then he blinks, looks at his own hand on your arm, and says it again, word for word, with the exact same wobble. A chalk slate hangs in the air above the pumps: THE HARBINGER, TAKE 9. He has been saying it all night.
signature.art: A wild-eyed old man in a trucker cap gripping a teenager's sleeve beside glowing gas pumps at eleven at night, a blank chalk slate hovering in the air under the fluorescent canopy, moths circling the lights, a humming ice machine, a station wagon parked at the pump with friends watching through the windows, white canopy light and dark road, medium shot

choices.label: Ask Mr. Hensley what he would actually say to you

success.text: "Forget the script," you say gently, "what do you really want to tell me?" His mouth works around the doomed line and swallows it. "Drive safe," he grumbles in his own voice, "and your back tire's low, I've been meaning to say." The slate over the pumps smears into a chalky thumbprint and drops to the asphalt.
success.art: An old man in a trucker cap and a teenager talking warmly beside gas pumps at night, a chalk slate crumbling into dust above them, warm fluorescent canopy light, a station wagon with a low back tire

failure.text: He grips harder. "Doomed," he insists, "doomed, doomed," and the slate clacks TAKE 10. Every time you open your mouth to answer, you hear yourself say "Whatever, old man" in a bored voice that is not yours, and you drive off with the line stuck in your teeth.
failure.art: A wild-eyed old man in a trucker cap clutching a teenager's sleeve under harsh gas station lights at night, a chalk slate clacking overhead, moths swirling around the canopy, rows of glowing pumps

choices.label: Read the script page in his pocket and refuse to play the end of the scene

success.text: You tug the page from his pocket. The scene ends with the teens laughing at him and driving off toward the camp, so you do the opposite: you buy him a coffee, sit on the curb beside him and stay put. A scene cannot end the way it is written if nobody leaves, and the slate gives up with a sulky clack.
success.art: A teenager and an old man in a trucker cap sitting on a gas station curb at night sharing paper cups of coffee, a crumpled script page on the asphalt, a drooping chalk slate overhead, glowing pumps

failure.text: The page holds one stage direction, in red: THEY IGNORE HIM AND DRIVE TO THEIR DOOM. Your hands steer the wagon onto the old camp road before you can stop them, and you end up somewhere dark and piney and much worse.
failure.art: A station wagon turning onto a dark pine-lined dirt road at night, headlights catching a rotting wooden camp archway, a frightened teenager gripping the wheel, a chalk slate floating in the back seat

choices.label: Yes-and him: get even more doomed than he is

success.text: "DOOMED?" you wail, dropping to your knees by the pumps. "Doomed by the curse of the Gas-N-Go hot dogs?" The night clerk laughs so hard he snorts, Mr. Hensley cackles, a real laugh, and the chalk slate cracks like a dropped plate. He presses two quarters into your hand for the air pump.
success.art: A teenager dramatically kneeling by a gas pump with arms flung wide at night, an old man in a trucker cap cackling, a clerk laughing in the shop doorway, a chalk slate cracking apart in midair

failure.text: You overdo it, and the slate loves it. A boom mic drops into view over the ice machine, a spotlight snaps on, and you and Mr. Hensley play the scene again and again, each take hammier, until sunrise finally sets you both free.
failure.art: A teenager and an old man in a trucker cap overacting under a hard white spotlight at a gas station at night, a boom microphone dangling above an ice machine, a glowing chalk slate

signature.title: Lovers' Lane
signature.text: Up at Glimmer Point, Denise Ocampo and Lorna Sykes from the softball team are sharing a milkshake in Denise's Thunderjet and watching the town lights, the way they do every week when they think nobody knows. Tonight the car radio cuts into their slow song with a bulletin about a hook-handed killer loose in the hills, the oldest campfire story in Glimmer Falls. The reel knows exactly how it wants this one to end, and it has the two girls typed in as the couple who goes first. A spotlight swings down out of the sky onto the Thunderjet. Across the valley, porch lights blink on all over town, as if everyone is tuning in.
signature.art: A cherry-red 1970s muscle car parked at a hilltop overlook at midnight, two teenage girls in softball jackets sharing one milkshake with two straws inside, the glittering lights of a small valley town below, a hard white spotlight beam stabbing down onto the car from the dark sky, a teenager running toward the car from a pay phone, wide shot

choices.label: Call KGLM from the pay phone and dedicate a love song to the Thunderjet

success.text: You sprint to the pay phone, and Mix puts you straight on the air: "This one goes out to the best couple on Glimmer Point, from all of us." The bulletin chokes off mid-word, the slow song swells back, and half the town hears the dedication. Denise and Lorna laugh so hard they spill the milkshake, and the spotlight slinks away like it got caught.
success.art: A teenager shouting happily into a roadside pay phone at night, a red 1970s muscle car nearby with two girls laughing inside and a spilled milkshake, a spotlight beam retreating into the sky, town lights twinkling below

failure.text: The pay phone plays you the hook bulletin too, in the same flat voice, and then the line goes dead. By the time you run back, the Thunderjet's windows are fogged with chalk dust and both girls sit frozen, staring straight ahead, waiting for a scratch on the roof. It takes the rest of the night to snap them out of it.
failure.art: A red 1970s muscle car with chalk-fogged windows at a midnight overlook, two frozen teenage girls staring ahead inside, a teenager running back from a pay phone, a hard spotlight pinning the car

choices.label: Walk right up and knock, so nobody screams at the wrong thing

success.text: You knock, wave and say, "It's just me. The radio is lying." Denise rolls down the window, Lorna shines a flashlight past you into the trees, and the three of you stand guard at the guardrail until the bulletin gives up. On the bumper you find a rubber hook from a costume shop, which is somehow the funniest thing all week.
success.art: Three teenagers standing guard at a hilltop guardrail at night beside a red 1970s muscle car, one sweeping a flashlight into dark pine trees, a rubber costume hook dangling from the bumper, town lights glowing below

failure.text: Your knuckles hit the glass at the exact moment the radio says "hook." Both girls scream, you scream, and so does something in the trees that is definitely not you. The Thunderjet peels out with you on the hood for twenty terrifying feet before you roll off into the gravel.
failure.art: A teenager clinging to the hood of a speeding red 1970s muscle car on a gravel overlook at night, two screaming girls behind the windshield, a spotlight swinging through dark pines, dust spraying from the tires

choices.label: Remind them how the hook story really ends: the couple drives away

success.text: "In every version, the couple drives away and lives," you shout. "Start the car!" Lorna turns the key, Denise floors it, and the Thunderjet roars down the mountain with you in the back seat, honking all the way. Behind you, the spotlight sweeps an empty overlook, hunting for an ending it is not going to get.
success.art: A red 1970s muscle car roaring down a winding mountain road at night with three laughing teens inside, headlights blazing, a lonely spotlight sweeping across a deserted hilltop overlook behind them

failure.text: You start the legend, and the reel finishes it in your mouth: "...and when they got home, there was a hook hanging from the door handle." Everybody screams, nobody drives, and the spotlight holds on the Thunderjet until dawn while the three of you huddle inside with the doors locked.
failure.art: Three frightened teenagers huddled inside a locked red 1970s muscle car at a hilltop overlook, a hard spotlight glaring through the windshield, pine trees swaying in the dark, the first gray of dawn on the horizon

signature.title: Final Girl
signature.place: Crystal Street, October 30, lit for the climax
signature.text: The night before Halloween, the reel shoots its climax on Crystal Street. Rain towers hiss over the lawns, a wind machine roars from the roundabout, and thunder sheets boom from the rooftops while your neighbors run in slow motion from a shadow that is never quite there. Then every light on the set swings onto you. The chalk slate writes FINAL GIRL: SURVIVES. ALONE, and you understand the deal: you get to live, as long as everyone else plays dead. Behind you, a camera crane rises over the street to catch your scream.
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac on the night before Halloween turned into a storm set, rain towers spraying over the lawns, a giant wind machine roaring beside a glowing purple crystal rock, neighbors in pajamas running in slow motion through the rain, a camera crane rising over the street, and every spotlight converging on one drenched teenager standing in the middle of the road, hard white light and rain, wide shot

choices.label: Do what a final girl never does: turn back for everyone else

success.text: You turn around and run back into the rain, grabbing hands, hauling neighbors up off the wet grass, shouting names until your voice cracks. A final girl only works alone, and you refuse to be alone. The slate's chalk runs in the rain until it reads FINAL GIRLS, then simply EVERYBODY, and the rain towers sputter dry.
success.art: A drenched teenager pulling neighbors of every age up from wet lawns in the rain, hands linked in a long chain down a suburban street, spotlights spreading wide, a chalk slate dripping in the downpour

failure.text: The slow motion catches you too. You run toward your neighbors for what feels like an hour, rain hanging in the air like glass beads, and never get closer. When the lights die, you are standing alone in the middle of the street, soaked, exactly where the script wanted you.
failure.art: A lone soaked teenager frozen mid-run in the middle of a suburban street at night, raindrops hanging in the air like glass beads, distant neighbors out of reach, a single spotlight overhead

choices.label: Give it a scream, all right: a scream queen's scream, on your own cue

success.text: Zelda taught you the trick: a real scream queen screams from the gut, on her own cue, never for the camera. You plant your feet and let loose a scream so huge and joyful it turns into a laugh halfway through. The crane shudders, its lens cracks, and the whole street stops running to applaud.
success.art: A teenager planted in the rain on a suburban street letting out a huge joyful scream that bursts into laughter, a camera crane shuddering above with a cracked lens, soaked neighbors applauding under spotlights

failure.text: Your scream comes out right on cue, thin and terrified, exactly the take the reel wanted. The crane swoops in for the close-up, the slate clacks PRINT IT, and you lose the rest of the night to that one scream looping in your ears.
failure.art: A camera crane swooping down for a close-up of a terrified screaming teenager in the rain at night, a chalk slate clacking beside the lens, harsh spotlights, a dark suburban street

choices.label: Find the junction box and shut down the weather

success.text: Every movie storm runs on one cable. You follow it across three lawns to a junction box behind the roundabout hedge and throw the big lever. The rain stops mid-drop, the wind machine whines down, and your neighbors stand blinking in an ordinary October night, dripping, confused and alive.
success.art: A teenager throwing a big lever on a junction box behind a hedge at night, rain freezing mid-fall over a suburban street, a wind machine spinning down, neighbors blinking in the sudden calm

failure.text: You throw the lever and get the effects crew's worst nightmare. The rain towers swivel and hose you from every direction at once, the wind machine blows you flat on a lawn, and up on the crane, the slate laughs in chalk.
failure.art: A teenager blasted flat on a soggy lawn by a roaring wind machine at night, rain towers spraying from every side, a camera crane looming above with a chalk slate perched on top

finale.title: The Final Cut
finale.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, Halloween midnight
finale.text: On Halloween the whole street ends up in the Glitter Box without remembering buying tickets. Every seat holds a neighbor in costume, every neighbor clutching sides with a role typed at the top. The Slate looms in the projector beam above the stage, chalk squealing out the last scene number. "Final reel," it booms. "Everybody knows how this ends." Up in the booth, Frankie Fontaine has her headset on, and in the aisle by row F, Celeste Navarro has stayed for the midnight show after all.
finale.art: A packed old movie palace on Halloween midnight, every seat filled with neighbors in costumes clutching typed pages, a towering figure of pale gold projector light and drifting film grain with a black-and-white clapperboard face and a chrome megaphone looming over the stage in the projector beam, four teenagers in homemade costumes standing in the center aisle facing it, a poised woman in cat-eye glasses standing in the aisle by them, a stage manager in a headset in the booth window, wide shot

choices.label: Storm the booth and smash the projector lamp

success.text: The lamp bursts in a shower of sparks. The beam dies mid-sentence and the Slate crumbles into a drift of chalk dust over the front rows. The neighbors blink, drop their sides and wander home confused. In the booth, the answer print is a melted lump on the reel.
success.art: A teen swinging a baseball bat into a theater projector lamp that bursts into sparks, the projector beam snapping out, chalk dust raining over the audience below

failure.text: The beam swings onto you before you reach the booth. For a long, grainy moment you are inside the movie, flickering at twenty-four frames a second, saying a line you never agreed to say.
failure.art: A teenager made of flickering black-and-white film grain on a giant movie screen, mouth open mid-line, the real theater audience staring up

choices.label: Splice the Saturday cartoons into the last reel

success.text: You splice a reel of cartoons into the slasher at the worst possible moment. The Slate bellows "ACTION!" and gets a coyote holding an anvil. It cannot do menace through a pie fight. The whole audience laughs as themselves, the beam sputters, and the cursed print unspools across the booth floor.
success.art: A movie screen showing a cartoon coyote with an anvil while a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure in the projector beam clutches its head, an audience in costumes laughing

failure.text: The splice holds for exactly four seconds. Then the tape gives, the cartoon burns away in a bubbling brown blot, and the Slate chalks TAKE TWO across the screen with a sound like nails on a blackboard.
failure.art: A movie screen with a spreading bubbling brown burn in the film, chalk scrawl appearing across it, a teen in the projection booth clutching a snapped strip of film

choices.label: Screen the ending they wrote, with Celeste in the room

success.text: Frankie threads the trims onto the reel. You hand the draft to Len and the call sheet to Celeste. Celeste takes the Slate's own megaphone and says, "Scene 88. Take one." On screen: dawn at Crystal Pines, Nurse Robin leading Duane, Kip and Cheryl out of the woods with the canoe on their shoulders, all four laughing. The neighbors sit back down as themselves. The Slate chalks THE END, and for the first time it means it.
success.art: A movie screen glowing with a sunrise film still of a nurse and three young campers carrying a canoe out of a pine forest, laughing, a woman in cat-eye glasses holding a megaphone in the aisle, a teen crew watching in awe

failure.text: The trims jam in the gate and the Slate's megaphone drowns Celeste out. You have every piece of the truth in your hands, but the reel needs threading more carefully than this.
failure.art: A theater projector with a strip of film jammed and buckling in its gate, a stage manager in a headset wrestling with it, a ghostly megaphone booming from the beam

choices.label: Go off-script, the way you did the first nights it handed you a part

success.text: "Hold it," you call from row F. "EXTRA #4 has notes." You ad-lib, and two hundred neighbors who remember being handed sides that first week start ad-libbing with you, heckling and yes-anding and talking back to the screen. The Slate cannot roll a single take with a whole house off-script, so its chalk squeals, the reel spins out of the gate, and the cursed print unspools across the booth floor like a party streamer.
success.art: A packed movie palace on Halloween night with costumed neighbors on their feet heckling a giant screen, a teenager standing on a seat in row F, a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure in the projector beam clutching its head, film unspooling like streamers

failure.text: You go off-script, but you go alone. The Slate swings its beam onto you, and the audience laughs on cue, a canned laugh that is not their own. You have the right idea; the house needs more than one heckler to drown out that megaphone.
failure.art: A lone teenager standing on a theater seat caught in a harsh projector beam, rows of costumed neighbors laughing with blank faces, a ghostly clapperboard-faced figure raising a megaphone overhead

choices.label: Storm the stage with the town behind you, the way you stood together when it came to your street

success.text: You march down the center aisle, and the neighbors who watched you stand up to it that week get up and march too, a whole street in one shot. You climb onto the stage, rip the megaphone out of the beam and hurl it into the orchestra pit. The Slate has nobody left to split up, and it crumbles into a drift of chalk over the footlights as the house lights come up warm.
success.art: A crowd of costumed neighbors marching arm in arm down a theater aisle behind a teenager who hurls a megaphone into the orchestra pit, a clapperboard-faced figure of light crumbling into chalk dust, warm house lights rising

failure.text: You start down the aisle, but the spotlights find the gaps between you and pick your neighbors off one by one, back into their seats with their sides clutched to their chests. You reach the stage steps alone and get shoved back by a blast of megaphone feedback.
failure.art: A teenager stumbling backward on theater stage steps from a blast of megaphone feedback, spotlights pinning costumed neighbors into their seats, a looming clapperboard-faced figure in a projector beam

choices.label: Refuse the last role it offers, like every role the night before, and give Celeste the spotlight

success.text: The beam swings onto you for the final twist, and you step out of it, the way you stepped out of every role it tried to staple on you the night before. "Not mine," you say, and you hold the call sheet up so the whole house can read the name: Celeste Navarro, Nurse Robin. Frankie threads the trims, Len hands Celeste his draft, and Celeste lifts the megaphone to call Scene 88, take one. Dawn breaks over Crystal Pines on the big screen, and everybody, on the screen and in the seats, walks out alive.
success.art: A poised woman in cat-eye glasses holding a megaphone in a theater aisle, a teenager stepping out of a spotlight beside her, a giant screen glowing with sunrise over a pine forest, costumed neighbors smiling in their seats

failure.text: You step out of the beam and hold up the call sheet, but the Slate's megaphone howls over Celeste's name before the house can hear it. The truth is in your hands. Hold it higher, and give her the room to say it herself.
failure.art: A teenager holding up a yellowed call sheet in a dark theater aisle, a ghostly megaphone blasting from a projector beam, a woman in cat-eye glasses beside them, costumed neighbors covering their ears

best.title: Curtain Call
best.text: The restored ending plays to a packed house, and everybody lives. When the lights come up, Glory pushes Celeste onto the stage and the Glitter Box gives her a standing ovation that lasts longer than the movie. Len stands in the back row and cries. Reggie Mabry, who played Duane, drives up from Sacramento the next weekend, and Donna Sayer and Tommy Kincaid call long distance. Frankie runs the writers' cut every Halloween after that, and the credits roll with one name restored: Nurse Robin, Celeste Navarro. She takes a bow every time.
best.art: A poised woman in her thirties with dark curls in a sequined gown and cat-eye glasses taking a bow center stage in a warm spotlight, red roses landing at her feet, a tall drag queen in a magenta sequin gown applauding beside her, a gentle man in a tweed blazer crying in the back row, the audience on its feet, a sunrise film still glowing on the movie screen behind, warm gold light, wide shot

good.title: Print Burned
good.text: The answer print is a melted lump and Crystal Street wakes up remembering nothing but a smell of hot popcorn. Next Saturday the Glitter Box runs cartoons. Celeste goes back to her crossword and never tells you what the movie was about. You keep a curl of melted film in your jacket pocket, and sometimes you wonder who it was really trying to hurt.
good.art: A teenager outside a small theater box office at dawn holding a curl of melted film up to the pink light, a woman in cat-eye glasses doing a crossword inside the glass booth, the marquee bulbs switched off above, a swept sidewalk, soft dawn light, medium shot

bittersweet.title: Rental Return
bittersweet.text: You survive the week, but the curse slips out on tape. Copies of the theatrical cut keep turning up in the Rewind Video night drop, and once in a while a neighbor hums the kill-order music without knowing why. Frankie cancels the midnight show for the season, and for the first time since 1981 the Glitter Box is dark on Saturdays. Celeste still sells tickets to the matinees. She still leaves before midnight.
bittersweet.art: A darkened theater marquee on a rainy Saturday night with its bulbs off, and down the wet sidewalk a lone woman in cat-eye glasses and a raincoat walking away under an umbrella, a video store window nearby with a bin of identical horror videotapes, reflections on the wet pavement, wide shot

bad.title: Extra #4
bad.text: On November first, your crew finds the cursed print still spooled in the booth, and when they run it you are in it: EXTRA #4, a flicker in the background of reel two, walking toward the boathouse forever. Every midnight showing, if they look closely, you wave. They keep buying tickets, and they keep trying to find the splice that will bring you home.
bad.art: A grainy black-and-white film projected on a movie palace screen showing a lakeside boathouse with a tiny teenager in the background waving toward the camera, three worried friends in the front row staring up at the screen, the projector beam above their heads, silver light, wide shot from behind the seats
